name: PORTRET
aliases: Physiotherapy OR TVT Randomised Efficacy Trial
question: Does initial midurethral sling surgery improve 12-month subjective improvement over initial pelvic floor muscle physiotherapy in women with moderate-to-severe stress urinary incontinence?

arms.label: initial supervised pelvic floor muscle physiotherapy, with crossover to surgery allowed

design.population: Women aged 35 to 80 years with moderate or severe stress urinary incontinence (stress predominant if mixed) at 4 university and 19 general hospitals in the Netherlands.
design.description: Multicenter pragmatic open-label randomized superiority trial

verdictNote: Surgery superior at 12 months; 49.0% of the physiotherapy group crossed over to surgery.
takeaway: In women with moderate-to-severe stress urinary incontinence, initial midurethral sling surgery gave higher 12-month subjective improvement than initial pelvic floor physiotherapy (90.8% versus 64.4%) in a modified intention-to-treat analysis; 49.0% of the physiotherapy group crossed over to surgery.

reports.label: 12-month randomized report
reports.citation: Labrie J, Berghmans BL, Fischer K, et al. Surgery versus physiotherapy for stress urinary incontinence. *N Engl J Med.* 2013;369(12):1124-1133.
reports.followUp: 12 months; outcome data for 196/215 (91.2%) surgery and 174/202 (86.1%) physiotherapy women analyzed

results.measure: 12-month subjective improvement (PGI-I much or very much better); absolute difference in percentage points, surgery minus physiotherapy
results.note: Modified intention-to-treat analysis with original data; with multiple imputation the difference was 26.5 points (95% CI 18.5 to 34.2; P<0.001).
results.locator: NEJM full text, Table 2; Results (Intention-to-treat analysis)

results.measure: 12-month subjective cure (no leakage with physical activity, coughing or sneezing on the UDI item); absolute difference in percentage points
results.locator: NEJM full text, Table 2; Results (Intention-to-treat analysis)

results.measure: 12-month objective cure (negative cough stress test at bladder volume of at least 300 mL); absolute difference in percentage points
results.locator: NEJM full text, Table 2; Results (Intention-to-treat analysis)

results.measure: 12-month PGI-S no symptoms; absolute difference in percentage points
Mean change in UDI urinary incontinence domain score at 12 months (0 to 100; lower is better)
results.note: Between-group effect size 0.50 (95% CI −1.6 to 2.6), described as moderate. UDI overactive bladder domain: −15.5 (SD 20.5) versus −10.6 (SD 19.5), P=0.02.
results.locator: NEJM full text, Table 2; Results (Intention-to-treat analysis)

results.measure: 12-month PGI-I improvement, post hoc per-protocol groups: initial surgery versus physiotherapy only; absolute difference in percentage points
results.note: Post hoc analysis. Women who crossed over to surgery after physiotherapy: 86/92 (93.5%); difference from physiotherapy only 61.8 points. P<0.001 for physiotherapy only versus either surgical group; P=0.68 for surgery after physiotherapy versus initial surgery. In physiotherapy-only women, subjective cure was 13/82 (15.9%) and objective cure 33/75 (44.0%).

harms.label: Bladder perforation
harms.note: Listed as a serious adverse event; P=0.03. Treated intraoperatively without further clinical implications. All adverse events in the physiotherapy group occurred in women who crossed over to surgery.

harms.label: Vaginal epithelial perforation
harms.note: Listed as a serious adverse event; treated successfully during surgery.

harms.label: Reoperation for tape exposure
harms.note: Six reoperations for tape exposure in total. One further woman (0.5% of the surgery group) needed reoperation to loosen the sling for persistent voiding problems.

harms.label: Blood loss of 500 mL or more
Any adverse event
harms.note: 65 adverse events in 41/417 women (9.8%); all were related to surgery.

delivery.label: Recruitment and sites
delivery.value: 656 women invited, 460 consented and were randomized (230 per group) between March 2008 and May 2010 at 4 university and 19 general hospitals.

delivery.label: Randomized and analyzed
delivery.value: Surgery group: 230 randomized, 15 withdrew consent before treatment, 215 underwent sling surgery. Physiotherapy group: 230 randomized, 28 did not start treatment (27 withdrew consent, 1 did not meet inclusion criteria), 202 started physiotherapy.

delivery.label: Surgeons and sling route
delivery.value: 49 gynecologists and urologists, each with at least 20 prior sling procedures; retropubic and transobturator routes were both allowed.

delivery.label: Physiotherapy regimen
delivery.value: Supervised pelvic floor muscle training by certified pelvic physiotherapists (83 of 478 in the Netherlands), building to 8 to 12 maximal contractions three times daily; intended nine sessions in 9 to 18 weeks; biofeedback or functional electrostimulation allowed.

delivery.label: Physiotherapy sessions attended
delivery.note: Mean sessions among women who crossed over to surgery after physiotherapy: 7.4 (SD 4.4); P=0.06 versus physiotherapy only.

delivery.label: Crossover from physiotherapy to surgery
delivery.note: 90/99 (90.9%) of these women reported no improvement on the last PGI-I before surgery. Crossover was similar with and without earlier specialized physiotherapy (18/38, 47.4% versus 81/164, 49.4%).

delivery.label: Additional physiotherapy after surgery
delivery.note: Training to relax the pelvic floor muscles for symptoms of pelvic floor hyperactivity such as obstructive micturition.

reports.label: 12-year questionnaire follow-up
reports.citation: van Oorschot HFC, Tijsseling D, Labrie J, van der Vaart CH. Twelve-year follow-up of a randomised controlled trial comparing the effectiveness of pelvic floor muscle training versus mid-urethral sling surgery for female moderate to severe urinary incontinence. *BJOG.* 2025;132(6):826-833.
reports.followUp: Mean 11.9 years (range 10.5 to 14.8); 184/386 (47.7%) women responded to a postal questionnaire

results.measure: Long-term PGI-I improvement, intention-to-treat, responders only; absolute difference in percentage points as printed in Table 1
results.note: No statistically significant difference. The report prints the difference and interval as −7.5 (−18.5 to 3.6); the surgery group's rate was higher (87.0% versus 79.5%).

results.measure: Long-term PGI-I improvement, intention-to-treat, all women with 12-month values carried forward for non-responders; absolute difference in percentage points
results.note: Last observation carried forward for non-responders; the authors state this may underestimate crossover or overestimate outcomes.
results.locator: Table 1; Results (Intention-to-treat analysis); Discussion (Strengths and limitations)

results.measure: Long-term subjective cure, all women; absolute difference in percentage points
results.note: Responders only: 66/91 (72.5%) versus 51/75 (68.0%), difference 4.5 points (95% CI −9.7 to 18.7; P=0.320).

results.measure: Long-term PGI-S no symptoms, all women; absolute difference in percentage points
Long-term PGI-I improvement, post hoc: initial surgery versus physiotherapy only, responders only; absolute difference in percentage points
results.note: Post hoc analysis. Surgery after physiotherapy: 62/72 (86.1%); difference from physiotherapy only 49.7 points (95% CI 25.8 to 73.7).

results.endpoint: PGI-I improvement, post hoc, all women
results.measure: Long-term PGI-I improvement, post hoc: initial surgery versus physiotherapy only, all women; absolute difference in percentage points
results.note: Post hoc analysis. Surgery after physiotherapy: 94/107 (87.9%); difference from physiotherapy only 63.3 points (95% CI 50.2 to 76.3).

harms.label: Urogenital reoperation after sling surgery

values.exp: 8/173 (4.6%) among responders who received a sling (both groups pooled)

harms.note: Five reoperations were for a surgical complication, two for recurrent incontinence and one for recurrence combined with a complication.

delivery.label: Crossover from physiotherapy to surgery, responders
delivery.note: At least 61.3% of all women crossed over, assuming the 61 non-responders who had physiotherapy only at 12 months did not. 6/100 (6%) of responders in the initial surgery group had additional physiotherapy.

delivery.label: Responders and exclusions
delivery.value: 386 women included (200 initial surgery, 186 initial physiotherapy); 184 responded (100 originally randomized to surgery, 84 to physiotherapy).
delivery.note: Of 417 women originally analyzed, 12 from centers with fewer than 4 inclusions were not approached; of 405 contacted, 7 had died and 12 declined.

relations.note: Physiotherapy before sling added nothing at 12 years; ESTEEM likewise found perioperative pelvic floor therapy gave no clinically significant symptom benefit over sling alone.
